title: The Kawangware Clinic That Needed a Small Lab: Ilara Health, 2019
dek: In 2019 a clinical officer told Emilian Popa he could not afford to test his patients, and Ilara Health set out to put devices in small Kenyan clinics on instalments.

story.event: Starting to place diagnostic devices in small Kenyan clinics on deposit and instalments
story.industry: diagnostics (point-of-care devices for primary care clinics)
story.summary: In early 2019 Emilian Popa met a clinical officer in Kawangware, Nairobi, who said he needed a small lab because he could not afford testing equipment and patients sent elsewhere often did not return. Ilara Health began placing portable diagnostic devices in small clinics for a deposit and 24 monthly payments, stalled at about 15 facilities while it trained clinicians to use the tests, then grew to about 3,000 clinics by 2024. In September 2025 it announced a significant staff reduction, citing market conditions and reversed funding commitments.
paragraphs: Early in 2019 Emilian Popa, who had spent four years at the venture firm DiGAME investing in African companies, met Dr Boniface, a clinical officer who ran a small clinic in Kawangware, on the edge of Nairobi, and dispensed medicines to his patients tablet by tablet. Popa asked what he would need to do his job better. As Popa later told it, the answer was a small lab: "If a patient needs a blood test, I can't do it because I can't afford the equipment." He sent those patients to a laboratory, and because of the cost of transport, many never came back.

Popa had been working on health ideas part-time for about six months, and went full-time that year. What he knew came from clinics more than from reports. Kenya had over 15,000 small primary care facilities, most with too few patients to justify a conventional analyser costing tens of thousands of dollars, and as informal businesses they had little access to ordinary small-business finance. A pilot that placed devices in five clinics showed that owners and staff wanted better tests but lacked the money and the technical skills.

The choice was to spread the cost of the machine. Ilara Health, which Popa co-founded with Maximilian Mancini and Sameer Afzal Farooqi, partnered with makers of small portable devices, many linked to mobile phones, for tests such as blood sugar, HbA1c and cholesterol. A clinic paid a small deposit and the balance over 24 months, and a device could be switched off remotely if payments stopped. The company was bootstrapped for six months, then raised a $735,000 seed round in 2019.

Then it stalled. "I was essentially building a business for which there was no market," Popa said; growth stopped at about 15 facilities, and Ilara had to train clinicians to see why the tests mattered. In 2020 he admitted that collecting the leasing fees was "not always obvious". By December 2020 it had more than 200 clinics in Nairobi and Kisumu and a $3.75 million Series A, and by 2024 about 3,000 clinics. In September 2025, citing market conditions and funding commitments that had been reversed, it announced a significant cut in staff. "This is a difficult moment for our team," Popa said.

quote.text: You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog,--the creature of a narrower sphere. You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect,--the creature of a season.
quote.locator: Chapter XVII, "Autumn Floods" (the Spirit of the Ocean to the Spirit of the River)
quote.source_title: Chuang Tzŭ: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, tr. Herbert A. Giles, Project Gutenberg eBook #59709
quote.connection: Popa admitted that he and his friends lived in a Nairobi bubble, barely aware of clinics ten or fifteen kilometres away. Zhuangzi's well-frog cannot be told about the ocean. What moved Popa out of his own well was not a report but one clinician's answer, and then hundreds of visits.

reflection: Popa's most useful early research was a single question put to one clinical officer: what would you need to do your job better? The payment plan, the training and even the stall all followed from taking the answer seriously, including its harder half. A device on a clinic counter is not yet a test that anyone orders or trusts.

You know that gap from the bench, and talQen sits inside it. When Ilara later said that quality of care, not access, was the issue in Kenya, it was describing ground you already work on. The habit worth keeping from this story is a small one: ask the person closest to the work, and listen hardest for the part of the answer you did not expect.
invitation: Ask one clinician or laboratory colleague today what single thing would help them do their job better this month. Write their answer down in their own words, and do not try to fix it yet.

cross_checks.claim: Ilara Health started in 2019 and raised a seed round that year.
The model: clinics got portable diagnostic devices through financing, paying over time.
Growth stalled at about 15 facilities before reaching more than 200 by December 2020.
A $3.75 million Series A led by TLcom in December 2020.
Co-founders are Emilian Popa, Maximilian Mancini and Sameer Afzal Farooqi.
About 3,000 clinics by 2024-25, and a staff reduction announced in September 2025.

research_notes: Co-founders: the slate's 'Kristin Griffin' is not supported by any source found. TechCrunch (2024) and Khusoko (2025) name Emilian Popa, Maximilian Mancini (co-CEO) and Sameer Afzal Farooqi (COO) as co-founders; a TechBuild Africa feature from about 2020 captions Farooqi as VP Operations and Mancini as Head of Strategy, and the 2020 funding releases name only Popa as co-founder, so the founder field gives Popa (whose own account the episode rests on) and the story uses the later co-founder description. The Dr Boniface exchange is Popa's own retelling in the Open Africa interview; the quoted line is as he rendered it. Clinic counts are taken from the dates given: 5 in the 2019 pilot and a stall at about 15 (Open Africa), 15 at the start of 2020 and more than 200 by December 2020 (NextBillion, Wamda), about 800 in February 2022 (Open Africa), about 3,000 in 2024 and 2025 (TechCrunch, Khusoko, HapaKenya). Patient numbers vary by date and basis (100,000 a month in 2022; more than 6 million a year in 2025, a company figure) and are left out. Funding: Open Africa gives a $735k seed in 2019 and close to $6m raised by 2022 across seed and Series A; Wamda dates the seed to August 2019; Khusoko calls the 2020 $3.75m round a seed round, while NextBillion and Wamda call it a Series A, which the story uses. The Gates grant is $1.1m in Wamda (2020) and $1.6m in grants in Khusoko (2025), probably cumulative; not used in the story. The 2025 cuts are reported as the company described them (market conditions, delayed funding and reversed commitments); the number of jobs lost was not disclosed, and no later outcome was found. Funding is set to venture although Ilara also used grants and debt. talQen is mentioned in this edition (the assignment allowed one mention, and the story is about diagnostics quality in Kenyan primary care).
